articles.title: The second-year quarterbacks who could break out during the 2026 NFL season
articles.standfirst: Examples of quarterbacks who excelled in their second season include Mahomes, Lamar, and Burrow
articles.summary: Examples of quarterbacks who excelled in their second season include Mahomes, Lamar, and Burrow
articles.body:
With the NFL regular season getting close it's a good time to remember that thru years second-year quarterbacks have exceeded expectations. Take for example Dan Marino in 1984 with 23 years winning the MVP after throwing for a record that lasted decades with 5,084 yards and 48 touchdowns while leading the Dolphins to the Super Bowl.

In more recent years Patrick Mahomes , also at 23 years, threw for 5,097 yards and 50 touchdowns becoming only the second player with such numbers (following Peyton Manning in 2013) and winning the MVP.

The year after Mahomes, Lamar Jackson also had an MVP season at 22 years old by being the first quarterback to throw for more than 3,000 yards (3,127) and rush for over 1,000 in a single season (1,206) . Or even last year, Drake Maye finished second in MVP voting after leading the Patriots to the Super Bowl against all odds

Sophomore Signal-Callers Primed to Take a Leap in 2026

Last season 14 quarterbacks were taken in the draft , but only three played over 10 games, and those three possess the best chances to stage a second-year breakout.

Cam Ward ( Titans ): The first overall pick in 2025 was the only rookie to play all 17 games, finishing with a rookie-high 3,169 yards and 15 passing touchdowns , though a 3-14 record resulted in the arrival of a new head coach in Robert Saleh and offensive coordinator Brian Daboll for this campaign.

Jaxson Dart ( Giants ): The 25th overall pick started 12 games, compiling a 4-8 record with 2,272 passing yards and 24 total touchdowns (15 passing) . He flashed immense dual-threat dynamism, though struggles with avoiding heavy hits cut parts of his debut season short. Armed with an experienced winning head coach in John Harbaugh and a reinforced roster, Dart enters 2026 with every tool needed for a stellar campaign.

Tyler Shough ( Saints ): Selected 40th overall, Shough wasn't originally slated to start in New Orleans, but after taking over the job in week eight he never looked back, finishing with a 5-4 record, 2,384 passing yards, 10 passing touchdowns , and a rookie-best 67.6% completion rate. Backed by a favorable schedule, Shough has all the momentum to guide the Saints toward the NFC South crown if the team remains healthy.

articles.title: Steve Gleason’s bedtime routine reveals a daily struggle most people never see
articles.standfirst: A video of the Saints legend’s bedtime care reveals an intimate part of life with ALS
articles.summary: A video of the Saints legend’s bedtime care reveals an intimate part of life with ALS
articles.body:
S teve Gleason shares what his bedtime routine looks like while living with ALS. The video shows his eyelids being carefully taped shut because he can no longer close his eyes on his own. It is a deeply personal glimpse of the help the former New Orleans Saints player needs to do something most of us take for granted: settle in for a night’s sleep.

It is an emotional scene, especially for football fans who remember him racing toward a punt in the Superdome. But Gleason has also spoken about what remains meaningful in his life. In an October interview with Good Morning America, he acknowledged the brutal days and described the joy of being with his family: “I get to love this life and the people in it.”

Steve Gleason’s eyes help him stay connected to the world

Steve was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, in 2011. The progressive disease affects the nerve cells that control voluntary muscle movement. Over time, it can take away a person’s ability to walk, speak, swallow and breathe independently. The needs and progression of the disease vary from person to person.

For Gleason, eye-tracking technology provides a way to communicate and write. Looking at a screen allows him to select letters and build sentences. He used that technology to write his memoir, A Life Impossible , with journalist Jeff Duncan. The process gave him a way to tell his story in his own words, but it also placed considerable demands on his eyes.

In a 2024 feature published by the Saints, Duncan described how Gleason’s difficulty blinking and closing his eyes interrupted their work. His care team would help him take breaks, using eye drops and medical tape while he rested. The report establishes that this challenge predates the circulating bedtime video. It also explains why caring for his eyes matters far beyond sleep.

That context makes the nighttime scene more personal. His eyes allow him to share an idea, send a message and take part in conversations. The person helping him close them is tending to a part of his body that carries much of his connection to everyday life.

Many Saints fans first came to know Gleason through one unforgettable play. On September 25, 2006, he blocked an Atlanta Falcons punt during New Orleans’ first game back at the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina. Curtis Deloatch recovered the ball for a touchdown. For a city still rebuilding, the moment became a lasting symbol of its return.

Twenty years later, Gleason returned for the team’s October 5 celebration with his family. His son, Rivers, pushed his wheelchair onto the field, and his wife, Michel, and daughter, Gray, joined them for photographs. The public celebration offered another view of the man seen in the bedtime clip: a father sharing an important night with his children and a former player still deeply connected to his city.

He has used that connection to help others. Steve and Michel founded Team Gleason after his diagnosis to support people living with ALS. The organization provides assistive technology, equipment and services, with the goal of helping people continue living meaningful lives. Its work recognizes that communication, mobility and access to care can change what someone is able to do each day.

Gleason continues to create, too. In his recent interview with Robin Roberts, he discussed Rebirth , a project pairing his poetry with New Orleans musicians. He also described life with a ventilator and the slow process of building sentences letter by letter. Those details make clear how much effort lies behind the words people hear from him.
